title: 3 Ways to Make Microservices Fail-Proof with Spring Boot (Retry, Circuit Breaker, Timeout)
description:
Have you ever clicked “Pay Now” in an app and nothing happens?
The page keeps loading… and then fails? 😩
In this video, I’ll show you how to fix that problem using Resilience patterns in Spring Boot.

You’ll learn:
✅ What causes these backend failures
✅ How to implement Retry, Circuit Breaker, and Timeout using Resilience4j
✅ Real-world examples in Java + Spring Boot
✅ When to use each pattern in microservices

Whether you're building a payment service, user API, or any microservice  these techniques will make your system more robust and reliable.

🔧 Code Examples Covered:
@Retry with fallback
@CircuitBreaker with fallback
@TimeLimiter + @CircuitBreaker for async with timeout
YAML config for timeout durations
👉 Don’t forget to Like, Subscribe, and hit the 🔔 bell for more Spring Boot tips!

transcript.text: Have you ever clicked pay now on an app
and nothing happens? This page keeps
loading 5 seconds, 10 seconds, then an
error message. Frustrating, right? This
usually happens when one service in the
back end fails or respond slowly. In a
micros service system, everything is
connected. If one service breaks, other
can fail too. So how do we stop that
from happening? In this video, I will
show you three smart ways to make your
microservices more reliable. Retry,
circuit breaker, time out. Let's start
with the first one. Sometimes a service
fails once but works fine if you try
again. This might be because of a small
network issue or a temporary error. This
is where retry helps. It means if the
first try fails, try again
automatically. Let's say your service
calls a payment API. If it fails the
first time, retry will try again maybe
two or three times before giving up.
Here we are using the retry annotation
from resilience. This method call
payment calls the payment service using
rest template. If this call fails,
Spring Boot will retry it automatically
based on the default settings, usually
three times. If all retries fail, it
will go back to the fallback method and
return a simple error message instead of
crashing. Now imagine the payment
service is not just failing once. It's
broken for a while. Retry again and
again won't help. It will just waste
time and overload the system. This is
where circuit breaker comes in. A
circuit breaker watches for repeated
failures. If a service keeps failing,
the breaker opens and blocks all future
calls for some time. After waiting a few
seconds, it tries one request. If it
works, the circuit closes and traffic
starts again. It just like an electric
circuit breaker at home. It trips when
there is a too much load, then resets.
This code uses the circuit breaker
annotation. If the call payment method
fails too many times in a row, let's say
five out of 10, this circuit opens and
for a short period, no more calls will
be made to the payment service. During
this time, any new calls go straight to
the fallback method. After a while, it
will retry one request again. If it
succeeds, the circuit closes. This helps
your app avoid calling broken services
again and again.
Now, let's say this service isn't
failing. It's just very slow. Waiting
too long can block your app and waste
resources.
That's where timeout comes in. It sets a
time limit. If a service doesn't respond
in time, the call is stopped. Imagine
calling customer care. If no one picks
up in 30 seconds, you hang up. That's a
timeout. In code, we set this using a
config file and annotation. Here we
configure 2 seconds timeout for the user
service in the EML file. That means if
the service takes more than 2 seconds to
respond, the call is canled. The method
returns a completable future which is
required by the time limiter to support
a sync timeouts. This protects your app
from getting stuck due to slow
responses. So let's quickly review. Use
retry when you expect temporary issues.
Use circuit breaker when a service keeps
failing and use timeout to stop long
slow calls. These three patterns make
your microservices stronger, faster, and
more reliable. Instead of crashing or
freezing, they help your app recover and
respond smartly. That's it. You have
just learned how to build resilient
microservices using retry, circuit
breaker, and time out. If you want more
Spring Boot examples or a full demo app
using these features, comment below.
